title: Severe Bleeding Control
summary: Immediately control life-threatening external hemorrhage using direct pressure and tourniquets.

steps.instruction: Ensure scene safety. Don PPE (gloves) if available.
Apply DIRECT PRESSURE with a clean cloth or bandage. Press firmly — do not release.
If blood soaks through, add MORE layers on top. Do NOT remove the first layer.
For limb wounds: If bleeding is not controlled in 2 minutes, apply a tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound.
Tighten tourniquet until bleeding stops. Note the time applied.
For neck/groin wounds: Pack the wound tightly with gauze. Apply sustained pressure.
Keep patient warm and lying down. Treat for shock.
Do NOT give food or water. Seek emergency care immediately.

warnings: Never remove a tourniquet once applied — only trained medical personnel should do so.
Femoral or axillary arterial bleeding can be fatal within 3 minutes.
Signs of shock: pale/cold skin, rapid weak pulse, confusion — treat urgently.

title: Adult CPR (30:2)
summary: Perform hands-only CPR for an unresponsive adult with no normal breathing.

steps.instruction: Check responsiveness: tap shoulders, shout 'Are you OK?'
Call for emergency services (or send someone to call).
Lay patient on a firm, flat surface. Tilt head back, lift chin — check breathing for no more than 10 seconds.
If not breathing normally: Begin chest compressions. Place heel of one hand on center of chest (lower half of sternum). Interlock fingers.
Compress HARD and FAST: at least 5 cm (2 inches) deep. Rate: 100–120 BPM. Allow full chest recoil.
After 30 compressions: Give 2 rescue breaths (1 second each, watch chest rise).
Continue 30:2 cycles without stopping until AED arrives, patient regains consciousness, or EMS takes over.
If AED is available: Power on and follow voice prompts immediately.

warnings: High-quality CPR: minimal interruptions, adequate depth and rate are critical for survival.
Do NOT delay compressions to find an AED — start CPR immediately.
If alone and unwilling/unable to give breaths, continuous hands-only compression at 100–120 BPM is acceptable.

title: Pediatric CPR (15:2)
summary: Perform CPR on an unresponsive infant or child using 15:2 ratio (two-rescuer).

steps.instruction: Check responsiveness: flick the bottom of the infant's foot or tap child's shoulders.
Call for emergency services.
Open airway: tilt head back slightly (less than adult), lift chin.
Check breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If absent or gasping: begin CPR.
INFANT: Use 2 fingers in center of chest, just below nipple line. Compress 4 cm (1.5 inches).
CHILD: Use 1–2 hands on lower sternum. Compress at least 5 cm (2 inches).
Rate: 100–120 BPM. Give 2 rescue breaths after every 15 compressions.
For infant rescue breaths: cover both mouth AND nose with your mouth. Gentle puffs only.

warnings: Pediatric cardiac arrest is most often due to respiratory failure — prioritize airway.
Do not tilt infant's head too far back — neutral position.
Infant breaths: blow just enough to see chest rise — do not over-inflate.

title: Choking — Adult (Heimlich Maneuver)
summary: Clear a foreign-body airway obstruction in a conscious adult.

steps.instruction: Confirm severe choking: Ask 'Are you choking?' If they cannot speak, cough, or breathe — act immediately.
Call for emergency services.
Stand behind the victim. Place one foot forward between their feet for stability.
Wrap your arms around their waist. Make a fist with one hand.
Place the thumb side of your fist against the abdomen — midway between navel and breastbone.
Grasp fist with other hand. Give FIRM inward-and-upward thrusts. Repeat until object is expelled.
If victim becomes unconscious: Lower them to the ground and begin CPR. Look in mouth before each breath.

warnings: Never perform blind finger sweeps — only remove object if you can see it.
For pregnant or obese victims: use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.
Partial obstruction: encourage forceful coughing — do not intervene yet.

title: Choking — Infant (Under 1 Year)
summary: Clear airway obstruction in an infant under 1 year using back blows and chest thrusts.

steps.instruction: Hold infant face-down on your forearm, supporting the head lower than the chest.
Give 5 FIRM back blows between shoulder blades with heel of your hand.
Turn infant face-up. Support head. Give 5 CHEST THRUSTS using 2 fingers on lower sternum.
Repeat back blows and chest thrusts until object is expelled or infant loses consciousness.
If infant becomes unconscious: Begin infant CPR. Look in mouth before each breath — remove object only if visible.

warnings: Never perform abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year.
Do not shake the infant.
Call emergency services immediately.

title: Anaphylaxis (Severe Allergic Reaction)
summary: Recognize and treat life-threatening anaphylactic shock immediately.

steps.instruction: Recognize signs: sudden hives/swelling, difficulty breathing, throat tightening, dizziness, rapid heartbeat after allergen exposure.
Call for emergency services IMMEDIATELY.
If patient has an epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen): Administer to outer thigh (through clothing is OK). Hold for 10 seconds.
Lay patient flat with legs elevated (unless breathing is difficult — then let them sit up).
If no improvement in 5–15 minutes and a second auto-injector is available: administer second dose.
If patient stops breathing: Begin CPR.
Keep patient warm. Do NOT give oral medications (swallowing may be impaired).

warnings: Epinephrine is the ONLY effective first-line treatment — antihistamines alone are NOT sufficient for anaphylaxis.
Biphasic reactions can occur 8–72 hours later — all anaphylaxis patients need hospital monitoring.
Symptoms can progress from mild to fatal in minutes.

title: Burns (Thermal)
summary: Assess and treat thermal burns. Cool the burn, protect the wound, prevent infection.

steps.instruction: Remove from source. Ensure scene safety — do not approach if fire/chemicals are active.
Cool the burn with cool (NOT cold/ice) running water for 20 minutes.
Remove jewelry and loose clothing near the burn — do NOT remove if stuck to skin.
Assess depth: Superficial (red, painful) / Partial thickness (blistering) / Full thickness (white/black, painless).
Cover with a clean, non-fluffy, non-adhesive dressing or cling wrap (loosely).
Do NOT burst blisters. Do NOT apply butter, toothpaste, or ice.
Seek emergency care for: burns >1% on face/hands/genitals, electrical burns, or any full-thickness burn.

warnings: Chemical burns: brush off dry chemical first, then irrigate with water for 20+ minutes.
Electrical burns may appear minor externally but cause massive internal damage.
Inhalation injury: hoarse voice, singed nose hairs, facial burns — high risk.

title: Fractures & Sprains (Splinting)
summary: Immobilize suspected fractures to prevent further injury and manage pain.

steps.instruction: Do NOT attempt to straighten or set the bone. Immobilize in position found.
Check circulation below injury: pulse, sensation, movement (capillary refill, skin color).
Apply splint: use padded rigid material (board, trekking pole, rolled newspaper). Extend splint beyond joints above and below the fracture.
Secure with bandages or strips — snug but NOT tight enough to cut circulation.
Elevate limb above heart level if possible. Apply ice pack wrapped in cloth (20 min on, 20 off).
Re-check circulation every 15 minutes. If pulse disappears or limb turns blue: loosen splint immediately.
For open (compound) fractures: cover wound with sterile dressing before splinting. Do NOT push bone back in.

warnings: Suspect spinal injury if: high-energy trauma, neck/back pain, numbness, or loss of bladder control — do NOT move.
A femur (thigh bone) fracture can cause 1–2 liters of blood loss internally.
Open fractures have high infection risk — cover wound immediately.

title: Head Injury & Concussion
summary: Assess and manage traumatic head injuries. Monitor neurological status closely.

steps.instruction: Stabilize the neck/spine if mechanism of injury was high-energy. Do not move patient unless in immediate danger.
Assess: Glasgow Coma Scale (Eye, Verbal, Motor). Note: confusion, unequal pupils, CSF from ears/nose.
If conscious: Keep calm and still. Assess orientation: name, date, location.
If unconscious with normal breathing: Recovery position (lateral recumbent). Monitor airway.
If not breathing: Begin CPR — maintain inline spinal stabilization.
Control scalp bleeding with direct pressure — scalp bleeds profusely but pressure is effective.
Do NOT give pain medications. Do NOT give food/water. Monitor every 15 minutes.
Seek immediate emergency care — worsening symptoms may indicate epidural hematoma (deteriorate fast).

warnings: DANGER signs requiring immediate evacuation: decreasing consciousness, one pupil dilated, seizures, worsening headache, repeated vomiting.
The lucid interval: patient may appear fine briefly then rapidly deteriorate — never leave alone.
All head injuries with LOC require professional evaluation.

title: Hypothermia
summary: Recognize and rewarm a victim of dangerous cold exposure.

steps.instruction: Remove from cold. Move to warm, dry shelter. Handle gently — do NOT rub vigorously.
Remove wet clothing. Replace with dry insulation layers. Wrap in blanket or sleeping bag.
Mild (shivering, alert): Give warm sweet drinks if fully conscious and swallowing is unimpaired.
Moderate (no shivering, confused): Apply chemical heat packs to armpits, groin, and neck. DO NOT apply directly to skin.
Severe (unconscious, rigid): Handle extremely carefully. Check pulse for 60 seconds before assuming absent.
If no pulse after 60-second check: Begin CPR. Continue until core rewarmed or EMS arrives.
'Not dead until warm and dead' — patients have survived prolonged CPR in hypothermia.

warnings: Rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation in severe hypothermia.
Do NOT give alcohol — causes vasodilation and worsens heat loss.
Active rewarming of limbs before core warms can cause afterdrop (sudden temperature drop).

title: Heat Stroke & Heat Exhaustion
summary: Recognize heat emergencies and rapidly cool the patient.

steps.instruction: Distinguish: Heat Exhaustion (sweating, pale, weak pulse) vs Heat Stroke (HOT dry skin, confusion, no sweating) — Heat Stroke is immediately life-threatening.
Move patient to cool shade or air-conditioned area immediately.
For Heat Stroke: Cool RAPIDLY. Apply ice packs to neck, armpits, groin. Wet skin and fan aggressively.
For Heat Exhaustion: Lay flat, elevate legs. Give cool fluids (water, electrolyte drinks) if conscious.
Remove excess clothing.
Call emergency services for Heat Stroke. Monitor consciousness every 5 minutes.
Do NOT give aspirin or acetaminophen for heat stroke fever — ineffective and potentially harmful.

warnings: Heat stroke core temp can exceed 40°C (104°F) — brain damage begins within minutes.
Cooling must begin BEFORE evacuation — every minute matters.
Elderly, infants, and those on diuretics/antipsychotics are high risk.

title: Animal Bites, Snake & Spider Envenomation
summary: Manage envenomation and animal bite wounds in the field.

steps.instruction: Move victim away from snake/animal. Note appearance for identification if safe.
Keep victim calm and still. Immobilize bitten limb at or below heart level.
Remove rings, watches, tight clothing near bite — swelling will occur.
Apply clean bandage. For pressure-immobilization (pressure bandage method) for neurotoxic snakes: wrap firmly from extremity upward.
Mark and note time of bite. Monitor: swelling spread, bruising, systemic symptoms (nausea, diplopia, difficulty breathing).
For bee stings: Remove stinger by scraping sideways. Apply cold pack. Monitor for anaphylaxis.
Evacuate immediately. Antivenom is the definitive treatment — field treatment is supportive only.

warnings: Do NOT cut and suck venom — ineffective and causes local tissue damage.
Do NOT apply tourniquet — worsens necrosis.
Do NOT apply electric shock — no evidence of benefit.
Antivenom timing is critical — transport immediately.

title: Seizures
summary: Protect the patient during a seizure and manage the post-ictal phase.

steps.instruction: Time the seizure. Protect from injury: clear surrounding area of hard/sharp objects.
Do NOT restrain. Do NOT put anything in mouth.
Cushion the head with something soft.
Loosen tight clothing around neck.
After seizure: Place in recovery position. Assess breathing. Stay until fully conscious.
Call emergency services if: seizure >5 minutes, second seizure occurs, no recovery of consciousness, injury, first-time seizure, pregnancy.
Reassure during post-ictal confusion — patient will be disoriented.

warnings: Status epilepticus (seizure >5 min or repeated without recovery) is a medical emergency.
Never put fingers or objects in the mouth — tongue biting is not preventable this way and you will be bitten.
Protect patient dignity — move bystanders back.

title: Asthma Attack
summary: Manage acute asthma attack and escalate severe attacks to emergency care.

steps.instruction: Keep patient calm and upright (sitting forward). Loosen clothing.
Help patient use their own rescue inhaler (salbutamol/albuterol): 1 puff, 4 breaths, repeat up to 4 puffs.
If using a spacer device: 1 puff into spacer, breathe 4–5 times, repeat.
Wait 4 minutes. If no improvement: repeat 4 puffs. Repeat cycle up to 3 times.
Call emergency services if: no relief after 12 puffs, lips/fingernails turn blue, unable to speak in full sentences, exhausted.
Severe: Continuous salbutamol every 20 minutes while awaiting EMS.

warnings: Silent chest (no wheeze) in severe asthma is a sign of near-fatal attack — call EMS immediately.
Avoid known triggers: exercise, cold air, allergens, smoke.
Oxygen via mask if available.

title: Suspected Spinal Injury
summary: Stabilize and protect a patient with suspected spinal cord injury.

steps.instruction: DO NOT MOVE the patient unless in immediate life-threatening danger (fire, drowning).
Stabilize head in neutral position: hold head between both hands, do not allow rotation or flexion.
If in water: Keep face above water, support head and neck in neutral position while extracting.
Assess neurological status: ask about numbness, tingling, or inability to move limbs.
If must move patient: Log-roll with minimum 3 rescuers, maintaining spinal alignment at all times.
Maintain manual stabilization until professional immobilization (rigid collar + spine board) is available.
Call emergency services. Continue to monitor ABCs.

warnings: Suspect spinal injury in: high-speed MVAs, falls from height, diving accidents, significant head/neck trauma.
An unstable cervical fracture with cord displacement can cause permanent paralysis or death.
Helmet removal: requires two rescuers, performed carefully only if necessary for airway.

title: Diabetic Emergency (Hypoglycemia)
summary: Recognize and treat dangerously low blood sugar in a diabetic patient.

steps.instruction: Recognize signs of hypoglycemia: shakiness, sweating, pale skin, confusion, irritability, rapid heart rate, hunger.
If patient is conscious and able to swallow: Give fast-acting sugar immediately.
15–20g of fast glucose: 4 glucose tablets, or 150mL fruit juice/regular soda, or 1 tablespoon of honey.
Wait 15 minutes. Re-check. If no improvement: repeat sugar dose.
Once improved: Give a more substantial snack (complex carb + protein) to stabilize.
If unconscious or unable to swallow: Do NOT give anything by mouth. Place in recovery position. Call EMS.
Glucagon injection (if available and trained): administer IM into thigh/buttock.

warnings: Never give food/drink to an unconscious patient — aspiration risk.
If unsure whether hypo or hyperglycemia: give sugar anyway — harmful only if hyperglycemic, but low risk vs benefit.
Severe hypoglycemia can cause seizures and permanent brain damage.

title: Stroke (FAST Assessment)
summary: Rapidly identify stroke using FAST and arrange emergency transport — time is brain.

steps.instruction: FACE: Ask patient to smile. Is one side drooping or uneven?
ARMS: Ask to raise both arms. Does one drift downward?
SPEECH: Ask to repeat a simple sentence. Is speech slurred, confused, or unable?
TIME: If ANY of the above are positive — call emergency services IMMEDIATELY. Note the exact time symptoms started.
Do NOT give food, water, or aspirin. Keep patient calm and still.
If conscious: Position in recovery position or supported sitting. If unconscious: manage airway.
Monitor vital signs every 5 minutes. Reassure constantly.

warnings: Thrombolysis (clot-busting) must be given within 4.5 hours — every minute of delay = 1.9 million neurons lost.
Do NOT give aspirin without medical instruction — hemorrhagic stroke would be worsened.
Even brief 'mini-strokes' (TIA) that resolve require immediate hospital evaluation.

title: Drowning
summary: Rescue and resuscitate a drowning victim.

steps.instruction: Scene safety first: Do NOT enter water without proper training/equipment. Use reach, throw, or row techniques.
Remove from water as quickly and safely as possible.
Check responsiveness and breathing immediately.
If not breathing: Give 5 rescue breaths FIRST (drowning is respiratory arrest — breaths are priority).
If no pulse after breaths: Begin CPR (30:2 adult / 15:2 pediatric).
Do NOT delay CPR attempting to drain water from lungs — begin compressions.
All near-drowning survivors require hospital evaluation — secondary drowning can occur 24 hours later.

warnings: Drowning is silent — victims rarely call for help.
Cold water submersion: may survive longer — continue CPR even after prolonged submersion in cold water.
All conscious drowning victims: lay flat, keep warm, seek emergency care.

title: Eye Injuries
summary: First aid for chemical splash, foreign bodies, and penetrating eye injuries.

steps.instruction: Chemical splash: irrigate IMMEDIATELY with large amounts of clean water for 20 minutes. Hold eye open under gentle stream.
Foreign body (non-penetrating): Do NOT rub. Pull upper lid over lower to allow tears to flush it. Irrigate.
Penetrating injury: Do NOT remove object. Shield the eye with a rigid cup — do not apply pressure.
Cover BOTH eyes (injured and uninjured) to minimize eye movement.
Keep patient calm and lying down. Seek emergency ophthalmology care.

warnings: Penetrating eye injuries: removing embedded objects risks vitreous humor loss and permanent blindness.
Alkali burns (bleach, cement) penetrate deeper and are more severe than acid burns — irrigate longer.
Any visual changes after trauma require urgent opthalmological evaluation.

title: Traumatic Amputation
summary: Control life-threatening hemorrhage and preserve amputated part for potential reimplantation.

steps.instruction: Apply tourniquet to stump IMMEDIATELY — high on limb, 5–7 cm above wound.
Tighten until bleeding stops. Note application time.
Cover stump with clean moist dressing. Continue monitoring for breakthrough bleeding.
Treat for shock: lay flat, elevate legs if no spinal injury, keep warm.
Preserve amputated part: wrap in moist clean cloth, place in a clean bag, then in ice water (NOT directly on ice).
Label bag with patient name and time of amputation. Transport with patient.
Fingers/digits reimplantation window: 6 hours warm / 12 hours cold. Larger limbs: 4 hours warm / 6 hours cold.

warnings: Life over limb — hemorrhage control is absolute priority over part preservation.
Do NOT place amputated part directly on ice — frostbite will make reimplantation impossible.
Call ahead to receiving hospital about potential reimplantation patient.
